quick: 250 mg PO QID or 500 mg q12h; up to 4 g/day
Best fasting (>=1/2-2 h before meals); may give with food
Use if needed; cardiovascular malformations reported in early pregnancy
Not dialyzed; monitor elderly for hearing loss
LFTs, ECG/QT if risk factors, CK with statins
summary: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibacterial that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis and is used for mild-to-moderate respiratory, skin, and other susceptible infections, as a penicillin alternative in allergic patients, and for chlamydial, pertussis, and diphtheria indications. Oral adult dosing is 250 mg four times daily or 500 mg every 12 hours, up to 4 g/day; pediatric dosing is 30-50 mg/kg/day in divided doses. It is a CYP3A4 substrate and inhibitor causing numerous serious drug interactions and is contraindicated with terfenadine, astemizole, cisapride, pimozide, ergot alkaloids, and simvastatin/lovastatin. Key risks include QT prolongation with torsades de pointes, hepatotoxicity, infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, and C. difficile colitis. Optimal blood levels occur in the fasting state.
indications: Upper respiratory tract infections (mild-moderate) due to S. pyogenes, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae (with sulfonamide)
Lower respiratory tract infections (mild-moderate) due to S. pyogenes or S. pneumoniae
Respiratory tract infections due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Skin and skin structure infections (mild-moderate) due to S. pyogenes or S. aureus
Pertussis (whooping cough) caused by Bordetella pertussis, and prophylaxis in exposed individuals
Diphtheria due to Corynebacterium diphtheriae (adjunct to antitoxin; carrier eradication)
Intestinal amebiasis caused by Entamoeba histolytica (oral only)
Acute pelvic inflammatory disease due to N. gonorrhoeae (penicillin-allergic, after IV erythromycin)
Chlamydia trachomatis infections: newborn conjunctivitis, infant pneumonia, urogenital infection in pregnancy, uncomplicated urethral/endocervical/rectal infection (when tetracyclines unsuitable)
Nongonococcal urethritis caused by Ureaplasma urealyticum (when tetracyclines unsuitable)
Primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) in penicillin-allergic patients (oral forms)
Legionnaires' Disease caused by Legionella pneumophila
Prophylaxis of initial and recurrent attacks of rheumatic fever in penicillin-allergic patients

dosage.d: 250 mg QID or 500 mg q12h; up to 4 g/day
dosage.n: Twice-daily dosing not recommended above 1 g/day

dosage.t: Equally divided; may double for severe infection

dosage.n: If not tolerated: 500 mg q12h or 250 mg QID for 14 days

dosage.d: IV 500 mg q6h x3 days, then 500 mg PO q12h x7 days

admin: Take by mouth in equally spaced doses
Optimal blood levels achieved in fasting state: at least 1/2 hour and preferably 2 hours before meals
May be dosed without regard to meals as erythromycin tablets are generally well absorbed
Complete the full prescribed course even if feeling better
Use only for proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection (stewardship)
Avoid concomitant contraindicated drugs (terfenadine, astemizole, cisapride, pimozide, ergot, simvastatin/lovastatin)
moa: Erythromycin inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by reversibly binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit of susceptible organisms, blocking peptide chain elongation; it does not affect nucleic acid synthesis. The effect is generally bacteriostatic. Resistance arises mainly through modification of the 23S rRNA in the 50S subunit, with efflux as an additional mechanism. In vitro antagonism exists between erythromycin and clindamycin, lincomycin, and chloramphenicol.

absolute: Concomitant terfenadine, astemizole, cisapride, or pimozide
Concomitant simvastatin or lovastatin (CYP3A4-metabolized statins) due to myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk
relative: Known QT prolongation or proarrhythmic conditions (uncorrected hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, significant bradycardia)
Concurrent Class IA (quinidine, procainamide) or Class III (dofetilide, amiodarone, sotalol) antiarrhythmics
monitor: Concomitant CYP3A4 substrates (colchicine, atorvastatin, calcium channel blockers, theophylline, digoxin, oral anticoagulants)
Elderly patients (QT effects, hearing loss, anticoagulant effect)

preg: No evidence of teratogenicity or embryotoxicity in animal reproduction studies. Observational human studies have reported cardiovascular malformations after exposure during early pregnancy. In treating syphilis during pregnancy, erythromycin may not reach the fetus in adequate concentration to prevent congenital syphilis; infants should be treated with an appropriate penicillin regimen.
lact: Erythromycin is excreted in human milk. Caution should be exercised when administered to a nursing woman.
renal: Erythromycin is not removed by peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis. Elderly patients, particularly those with reduced renal function, may be at increased risk for erythromycin-induced hearing loss.
hepatic: Since erythromycin is principally excreted by the liver, caution should be exercised in patients with impaired hepatic function. The effect of hepatic dysfunction on biliary excretion of erythromycin is not known.

major: Terfenadine, astemizole, cisapride, pimozide - QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, fatalities (contraindicated)
Ergotamine/dihydroergotamine - acute ergot toxicity with vasospasm/ischemia (contraindicated)
Colchicine - life-threatening colchicine toxicity; reduce colchicine dose
Class IA/III antiarrhythmics (quinidine, amiodarone, sotalol) - additive QT prolongation
moderate: Theophylline - increased theophylline levels/toxicity; erythromycin levels may fall ~35%
Calcium channel blockers (verapamil, amlodipine, diltiazem) - hypotension, bradyarrhythmia, lactic acidosis
Oral anticoagulants (warfarin) - increased anticoagulant effect, more pronounced in elderly
Triazolam/midazolam/alprazolam - decreased clearance, increased benzodiazepine effect
Sildenafil - increased AUC; reduce sildenafil dose
Cyclosporine, tacrolimus, carbamazepine, rifabutin, quinidine, cilostazol, vinblastine, bromocriptine, disopyramide, alfentanil, methylprednisolone - CYP3A interactions
minor: Hexobarbital, phenytoin, valproate - altered metabolism (not via CYP3A)
Clindamycin, lincomycin, chloramphenicol - in vitro antagonism
interactions.food: Optimal blood levels obtained in the fasting state (at least 1/2-2 hours before meals); tablets may otherwise be taken without regard to meals.
interactions.alcohol: No specific alcohol interaction described in the label.
interactions.diagnostics: Interferes with the fluorometric determination of urinary catecholamines.

serious: Hepatotoxicity (hepatocellular and/or cholestatic hepatitis with or without jaundice)
Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) in infants
rare: Reversible hearing loss (high doses or renal insufficiency)
emergency: Torsades de pointes / ventricular tachycardia / cardiac arrest (fatalities reported)
Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis

monitoring: Liver function / symptoms of hepatitis during therapy
ECG / QT interval in patients with cardiac risk factors or proarrhythmic conditions
Serum potassium and magnesium (correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia before therapy)
Creatine kinase and transaminases if co-administered with lovastatin/statins
Theophylline and digoxin serum levels and INR (anticoagulants) when co-administered
Infants for non-bilious vomiting or feeding irritability (IHPS)
Signs of C. difficile diarrhea during and after therapy
counsel: Take exactly as directed and complete the full course even if feeling better
Best absorbed on an empty stomach (1/2-2 hours before meals)
Antibiotics do not treat viral infections such as the common cold
Report watery or bloody stools, which can occur up to two or more months after the last dose
Parents should contact their physician if an infant develops vomiting or irritability with feeding
Tell your provider about all medicines, especially heart-rhythm drugs, statins, ergot drugs, and colchicine
pk: Bacteriostatic; absorbed readily in microbiologically active form
Optimal blood levels in fasting state (1/2-2 h before meals)
Dosed QID or q12h; largely protein-bound, biliary excretion
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); excursions 15-30 C permitted
pearls: CYP3A4 substrate and inhibitor - screen for major interactions before prescribing (statins, ergot, colchicine, CCBs, theophylline, warfarin)
Contraindicated with terfenadine, astemizole, cisapride, pimozide, ergot alkaloids, and simvastatin/lovastatin
Avoid in known QT prolongation; correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia first; elderly are more susceptible to torsades
IHPS risk in infants - weigh benefit against risk, especially with pertussis prophylaxis (reported 5-10% risk)
Optimal serum levels in the fasting state; GI side effects are dose-related
Not removed by peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis
Penicillin alternative for strep pharyngitis, rheumatic fever prophylaxis, and primary syphilis in allergic patients
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule. Do not double the dose. Complete the full course of therapy.
overdose: Discontinue erythromycin. Promptly eliminate unabsorbed drug and institute other appropriate supportive measures. Erythromycin is not removed by peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis.
